To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
maternal separation, an animal model of early life stress (ELS) increased the number of midbrain dopaminergic neurons during early development in male rats.

maternal separation (MS), a model of early-life stress, increases the survival of neurons in the ventral tegmental and the substantia nigral pars compacta in male rats, which may be associated with sex-specific changes in the dopaminergic reward circuitry.

early life stress (ELS) induced sex‐dependent changes in the survival of dopaminergic and non‐dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental and substantia nigra area of the rat midbrain during postnatal development, and that ELS induced sex‐dependent behavioral changes related to the dopaminergic reward system in adult rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms underlying sex‐related differences in the vulnerability of dopaminergic neurons and reward‐related behaviors after ELS.
the mechanisms of the long‐term effect of ELS, which may help to develop new strategies for the prevention and treatment of neuropsychiatric diseases.
the effect of early-life stress (ELS) on the development of the midbrain dopamine system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the ELS increases the survival of dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain of males during postnatal development, and that this increase is accompanied by sex‐specific changes in reward‐related and anxiolyte‐like behaviors.
ELS induces sex‐specific dysregulation of midbrain dopaminergic circuits, which may lead, at least in part, to the sex‐specific psychopatology of the reward system.
ELS induces permanent changes in the number of midbrain neurons, which may be associated with sex‐dependent alterations in the reward system and anxiety behavior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ELS induces a permanent increase in the number and survival of dopaminergic and non‐dopamine neurons in the VtA of males.
ELS increases the survival of neurons in the VtA, but only in males, and that this effect is associated with a decrease in anxiety‐like behavior and increased preference for sucrose in adult males.
ELS increases the survival of non-dopaminergic neurons in the Vta and SNC of male offspring, which may lead the development of psychopathology of reward system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ELS may induce a sex‐specific dysregulation in dopaminergic neurons of the mesolimbic system.
ELS induces sex‐dependent changes in the midbrain dopaminergic system, which may lead the development of sex‐specific psychopatology of the reward system.
ELS can induce permanent and temporary changes in the number of midbrain neurons.
